title: GPU clocking and KV cache fragmentation -- experiments & notes
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working note capturing a sequence of small experiments and observations aimed at reducing KV cache fragmentation and improving latency predictability while using aggressive GPU clocking and power caps across A100/H100/L4/MI300 fleets. The aim: find low-risk knobs we can expose in the runtime to get per-query tail improvements without large throughput regressions. This doc is intentionally pragmatic: quick experiments, hypotheses, and recommended follow-ups.

Context and motivating signal:
- We see transient p99 spikes when mixed workloads run on node pools with heterogeneous KV residency (long-lived chat sessions + bursty generation).
- Thermal headroom and DVFS interactions appear to affect kernel selection fallback frequency; when clocks are high but power limited a few kernels revert to slower codepaths, producing long tails.

High-level hypotheses:
1) KV cache fragmentation (many small cached prefixes across many models) increases memory pressure and causes greater kernel-to-kernel variability when kernel fallback happens during thermal throttling.
2) Moderate power-capping (5-10% under nominal) plus a small reduction in sustained SM clocks can reduce fallback oscillation and lower p99 for short queries without harming throughput for long-sequence batches.
3) Strategic placement of hot prefixes into a "KV slab" (co-locating high-hit prefixes in contiguous pages) will reduce memory eviction churn and improve locality for KV reads, reducing kernel path divergence.

Experiment 1: baseline measurement (mixed chat + generation)
- hardware: H100 (PCIe) and A100 (NVLink), identical software stack (runtime v0.38.x), model mix: 60% chat-like (context length 512, short outputs), 40% generation (context 1024, long outputs).
- workload: 10k queries over 30m, client qps ramp 200->600, mixed sizes.
- metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, kernel-fallback-events (instrumented), KV hit rate, page-faults (host-visible).
- baseline results (median across 3 runs): H100 p99=290ms, A100 p99=310ms, KV hit rate=72%, kernel-fallback-events ~ 18/hr per GPU.
Observations: fallback events correlate with short bursts of high single-GPU power draw; KV hit rate dips when many chat sessions interleave.

Experiment 2: power cap delta and clock headroom window
- change: set power cap to 92% nominal TDP, reduce sustained SM clock target by -5% (via driver governor), allow burst window of 8s where clocks can ramp to nominal for short bursts.
- rationale: avoid repeated kernel LO->HI fallback churn while still allowing bursts to complete fast.
- results: p99 dropped to 210ms (H100) and 225ms (A100); throughput reduced by 1.8% for long sequence batches; kernel-fallback-events dropped to ~6/hr. KV hit rate unchanged.
- notes: the 8s window seems to let short chat replies finish in boosted mode; longer generation requests occasionally hit fallback during sustained periods but overall system behaved more stable.

Experiment 3: KV slabting (software experiment)
- change: runtime organizes KV cache into 4 logical slabs by prefix-hotness; hot slab pinned to GPU memory region with preferred affinity and eviction policy LRU-2; cold slab allowed to spill earlier. Allocation uses an allocator flag to try to allocate contiguous physical pages (best-effort).
- test: same mixed workload with baseline clocks (no power cap change).
- results: KV hit rate increased to 78%; p99 improved modestly (H100 270ms), kernel-fallback-events unchanged. Notable reduction in host-visible page faults.
- caveat: contiguous physical allocation isn't guaranteed on long-running nodes; works best on freshly provisioned instances.

Experiment 4: combined knobs (KV slab + gentle power cap + burst window)
- change: apply KV slabting + power cap at 92% + -5% sustained clock + 8s burst window.
- results: p99 H100=185ms, A100=198ms; throughput loss ~2.2% on long sequences but tokens/sec for mixed workload improved slightly because fewer tail outliers. Kernel-fallback-events <4/hr. KV hit rate 81%.
- qualitative: system feels much 'smoother' in telemetry; spike-related traces are shorter.

Micro observation: L4 and MI300 behavior
- L4 (edge inference style): lower thermal headroom but simpler kernel paths; reducing sustained clocks hurt throughput more (up to 6% for batch workloads) so recommend conservative power caps (>=97%) and focus more on KV layout optimizations.
- MI300: high-bandwidth HBM behavior means KV eviction is cheaper in-memory, but driver/ROCm kernel selection appears brittle when clocks bounce; KV slabting plus a slightly larger burst window (12s) gave best results on MI300 in our runs.

Kernel selection notes and telemetry hooks suggested:
- Add a short-lived kernel-stability score per device that decays over 60s. If score drops (due to fallback anomalies), runtime should reduce concurrent active kernels for a short window or prefer stable kernels.
- Emit per-request kernel-choice metadata into traces to analyze which model shapes tend to trigger fallback.

Operational rules-of-thumb we can adopt immediately:
- For mixed chat-heavy pools on H100/A100, try power cap 90-94% with small burst windows (6-10s) and -3 to -7% sustained clock targets. Start conservatively and raise if throughput-sensitive models suffer.
- For edge L4 pools, prefer KV layout changes over clock reduction; power cap >=97%.
- For MI300, allow slightly longer burst windows (10-14s) before dropping clocks.
- Fresh node provisioning improves contiguous allocation success for KV slabting. Consider a low-fragmentation allocator run at boot time.

Outstanding questions / follow-ups:
- How to detect live which cached prefixes are "hot" reliably without expensive telemetry? (sampling vs full counters).
- Could we implement a background compaction/defragmenter that moves hot prefixes together during low utilization? Risk: pointer-churn and transient performance cost.
- Scheduler integration: should we prefer routing short chat queries to nodes currently in boosted window? Risk: skewed utilization.
- Safety: need experiments for thermal worst-case and boss-level SLA implications of sustained power-capping.

Action items (who / when):
- Lina: prototype background KV compaction (best-effort) and run on staging fleet by 2025-03-21.
- Marco: add kernel-choice trace tags and instrument kernel-fallback counters in runtime by 2025-03-10.
- Priya: run 24h stability test with combined knobs on mixed H100 pool and produce a shared dashboard by 2025-03-12.
- Ops: consider node bootstrap script to run a quick defrag/allocator pass on new instances.

Appendix: quick config snippets (driver/runtime knobs)
- power cap example: nvidia-smi -i <gpu> -pl <TDP * 0.92> (apply via node boot script)
- clock governor: set sustained_sm_target = nominal * 0.95 (vendor API / runtime flag)
- burst window: runtime flag --clock-burst-window-seconds=8 (experimental)
- KV slabting: runtime config { kv_slab_enabled: true, slab_count: 4, slab_eviction: "lru2", allocator_hint: "contiguous_if_possible" }

Closing notes:
This is a pragmatic set of experiments showing that modest coordinated changes across power management and software layout reduce tail latency while keeping throughput largely intact. The biggest operational win was the smoothing effect of a burst window plus KV locality improvements. Next steps are to harden the KV slab allocator and add better telemetry to make these knobs safe to roll out in Dedicated and Hosted pools.

End of note.
